vignette:
Karim is a 54-year-old community organizer, married for nearly twenty years, who came to therapy at his wife's urging after months of escalating distress. The trauma that reshaped his life occurred eight years ago, before his current marriage, when he was in a relationship with a man named Tarek. One night, in the dimly lit basement apartment they shared, an argument over a misunderstanding turned violent. Tarek's hands closed around Karim's throat; his voice was a low, cold whisper that Karim can still hear, word for word, as if it were recorded in his skull. The assault lasted only a few minutes, but what Karim remembers comes in jumbled pieces-the pressure on his windpipe, the sting of his own teeth cutting his cheek when his head hit the wall, a single, almost surreal detail: the distant thwop-thwop-thwop of a helicopter passing overhead that he fixated on as he tried not to lose consciousness. He managed to push Tarek away and escape, and he never returned to that apartment. The relationship ended, but the event never left him.

In the weeks and months afterward, Karim found himself unable to walk down the block where the basement apartment had been. He took a different bus route, added thirty minutes to his commute, and eventually stopped going to the neighborhood altogether. That part of the city became a forbidden zone in his mind. At home, he began to wear clothes that made him feel invisible-oversized jackets, dark colors, hoods that shadowed his face. He told himself it was just comfort, but he had come to believe that if he looked nondescript enough, no one would notice him, and if no one noticed him, no one would hurt him. The darkness of evening became a particular dread. He insisted on keeping lights on in every room, even while sleeping, and his wife learned not to turn off the hallway lamp. When she asked why, Karim could only say he didn't like the dark.

The helicopter sound became a recurring torment. Once, while out at a community picnic he had organized, a news helicopter flew overhead, and the rotors hit him like a physical blow-the full memory crashed over him without warning, fragmentary and overwhelming: the whisper, the pressure, the wall. He froze, dropped the plate he was holding, and excused himself to sit shaking in his car for twenty minutes. After that, he began scanning the sky whenever he heard an aircraft, his body tensing, his mind racing. More broadly, he became hypervigilant toward people-anyone who seemed too large, too close, too angry. He would study strangers' hands, their tone of voice, the way they moved. He was certain that danger could come from anyone, because it had come from someone he had once trusted completely. The betrayal had shattered something fundamental: Karim now believed that his own judgment of character was worthless, that he had somehow attracted the abuse because of who he was, that the world was not a place where kindness existed behind closed doors.

His work as a community organizer suffered silently. He avoided evening events, refused to go to certain blocks for outreach, and began delegating home visits to colleagues. His wife noticed he was pulling away from friends and that his once-warm laugh had become rare. What finally brought him to therapy was a panic attack in a darkened parking garage-he had to crouch between two cars, sweating, certain that someone was coming for him, the fragmented echoes of Tarek's whisper drowning out the rational part of his mind. He is afraid that he is losing himself, and he hopes, with quiet desperation, to find a way to feel safe in his own life again.
